items.prompt: Cost in an architecture is best described as which kind of requirement?
choices: A purely functional requirement of the product
A legal requirement written by the lawyers
A marketing requirement for the launch
items.explanation: Cost sits beside latency and availability as a quality the design must meet.

items.prompt: Where does a cost failure usually first show up?
items.explanation: Cost fails on a slower clock than outages: invoices arrive monthly.

items.prompt: A service answers every request correctly. Can it still have failed as a design?
choices: No, cost is a finance matter
Yes, but only if it is slow
Yes, if it is too costly to sustain
items.explanation: Correctness is necessary but not sufficient.

items.prompt: Which pair names requirements of the same family as cost?
items.explanation: All three are qualities of how the system performs, not what it does.

items.prompt: Why did GreenCart's finance team treat the sale bill as an incident?
choices: Some of the orders were processed wrongly
Cost per order rose sharply as volume grew
Checkout was down for hours during the sale
The sale ran longer than the team planned
items.explanation: Nothing was wrong functionally; the economics were.

items.prompt: Which statement about cost failures is true?
choices: They are discovered later than outages
They always trigger a loud alert at once
items.explanation: No monitor fires; the invoice is the signal.

items.prompt: Who can influence cost at design time?
choices: Only the billing department's own staff
items.explanation: Cost curves are largely set by architecture before launch.

items.prompt: A design is fast and correct but unaffordable at scale. What is the fair verdict?
choices: It passed, since it is fast
It passed, since it is correct
It failed one of its requirements
items.explanation: Meeting two of three requirements is still missing one.

items.prompt: A launch is fast, correct and fully available, yet its running cost doubles with each new customer cohort. What is the most accurate description?
choices: The only real issue is a gap in monitoring coverage
The team should add many more load tests first
A cost requirement was never designed for
It is a vendor billing error to dispute formally
items.explanation: Latency and availability passed, but the cost requirement was left unspecified, so the design failed on that axis.
items.reference:
Same family of requirements
⚡ latency: fails on a monitor in seconds
🟢 availability: fails on a monitor in minutes
💸 cost: fails on an invoice in weeks
Why: cost is a non-functional requirement; it only differs in how late the failure shows up.
items.learnMore:
Correct is not the whole bar

A design is judged on whether it does the job and whether it can keep doing it at a price the business can sustain. The failure is slow but real.

Common mistake

Treating the bill as someone else's problem because no alert fired.
items.reflection: Think of a habit or subscription that worked fine every day but quietly became unaffordable. What was the first signal you noticed?

items.prompt: Why is a cost failure harder to catch than a latency failure?
choices: Cost cannot be measured per service in the cloud
No monitor fires; the signal is a delayed invoice
Latency tests are always more thorough than cost
Cost depends only on which provider is chosen today
items.explanation: Feedback arrives on a monthly clock unless the team builds cost visibility.

items.prompt: Which metric best shows an architecture is not scaling economically?
choices: Total spend going up by any amount at all, ever
Cost per unit of value rising with volume
items.explanation: Spend naturally grows with the business; cost per unit should not.

items.prompt: Spend rose 2x while orders rose 6x. What happened to cost per order?
items.explanation: 2 divided by 6 is one third of the old ratio.

items.prompt: Which is a valid 'unit of value' for cost per unit?
items.explanation: The unit must track what the business sells.

items.prompt: Total spend doubling is, on its own, usually...
choices: Not enough to judge the design
items.explanation: You need the volume to interpret it.

items.prompt: GreenCart's cost per order went from $0.04 to $0.11. By what factor?
items.explanation: 0.11 divided by 0.04 is 2.75.

items.prompt: Which pair lets you compute cost per order?
choices: Number of orders and server names
Total bill and number of orders
items.explanation: Divide the bill by the orders.

items.prompt: Healthy scaling means cost per unit tends to...
choices: Rise steadily in step with volume growth
Fall or stay flat as volume grows
items.explanation: Fixed costs get spread over more units.

items.prompt: Revenue grew 6x and the bill grew 16.5x. The bill grew...
items.explanation: 16.5 is larger than 6.

items.prompt: Orders grow 4x and the bill grows 3x. What is the correct reading?
choices: Cost per order rose by a quarter of before
Cost per order is unchanged from before
Nothing can be said without latency data
Cost per order fell to 75% of before
items.explanation: 3 divided by 4 is 0.75, so the design is scaling economically.
items.reference:
Total spend vs. cost per unit
📊 spend up 2x, orders up 6x: cost per order falls (healthy)
🚨 spend up 16.5x, orders up 6x: cost per order rises 2.75x (warning)
Why: growing spend is fine; growing cost per unit means the design does not scale in money.
items.learnMore:
Divide by the thing the business sells

Pick the unit that tracks value: orders, active users, GB processed. Then watch the ratio, not the absolute bill.

Common mistake

Reading a rising total as a failure even when volume rose faster.
items.reflection: Pick a monthly cost in your life (commute, groceries). What is the 'unit' that would tell you whether it is getting more efficient or just bigger?

items.prompt: Bill up 10x, orders up 10x, cost per order flat. What does that suggest?
choices: The design is scaling badly in money terms
Fixed costs dominate the bill at this volume
Costs scale in exact proportion to volume
The orders were counted wrongly this month
items.explanation: Flat unit cost means no economies of scale and no diseconomies: fully proportional.

items.prompt: Which pricing model needs no commitment but can be reclaimed at any time?
items.explanation: Spot capacity is cheap because the provider can take it back.

items.prompt: Which model suits a steady, predictable baseline?
items.explanation: Predictable use makes a commitment safe.

items.prompt: Which work is safe to put on spot capacity?
items.explanation: Interruptions are harmless if work can be retried.

items.prompt: Which model is cheap at low volume and spiky traffic?
items.explanation: You pay only when requests arrive.

items.prompt: What does on-demand charge you for?
items.explanation: On-demand is pay per use, with no commitment.

items.prompt: What does reserved capacity charge you for?
items.explanation: The commitment is paid regardless of use.

items.prompt: GreenCart's failure was best described as...
choices: Using only on-demand for a predictable floor
items.explanation: A predictable floor should have been committed.

items.prompt: For a system with a floor and occasional spikes, the usual answer is...
choices: A blend of models by segment
items.explanation: Each segment has different predictability.

items.prompt: A nightly report job can pause and resume at any point and is safe to rerun. Which model fits it best?
choices: Spot capacity, since interruption costs little
Reserved capacity, to guarantee the hours it needs
On-demand capacity, to avoid every possible risk
Serverless, to scale all the way down to zero
items.explanation: Interruptible, retry-safe work is the ideal spot workload; the discount costs nothing in correctness.
items.reference:
Match the model to the load
📦 steady baseline: reserved / committed
🔁 interruptible, retry-safe: spot
🌙 near-zero baseline, spiky: serverless
🔧 the rest: on-demand with autoscaling
Why: each discount is bought with a constraint, so each workload segment gets the model whose constraint it can live with.
items.learnMore:
A blend, not a pick

Most systems have a floor, a middle and edges, and each can use a different model. The floor is committed, the middle autoscaled, the edges spot or serverless.

Common mistake

Choosing one model for the whole system.
items.reflection: Think of how you pay for transport: a monthly pass, a taxi, a rental. Which of your trips match each, and what happens if you buy the pass for a trip you rarely take?

items.prompt: A service runs at about 30 requests a second all day and spikes to 300 for an hour on some days. What is the best split?
choices: Commit capacity for the whole 300 peak, all day, every day
Run all of the traffic on spot instances to cut prices
Put only the spikes on reserved capacity, not the floor
Commit the 30 baseline, autoscale the spikes on demand
items.explanation: Commit what is always there; keep the unpredictable part elastic.

items.prompt: In cost per order = fixed / orders + variable, what happens to the first term as orders grow?
items.explanation: The same fixed amount is divided by more orders.

items.prompt: If the variable cost per order is constant, cost per order trends toward...
items.explanation: The fixed share vanishes, leaving the variable term.

items.prompt: What is 'economies of scale' in this model?
choices: Unit cost rises as volume grows
Unit cost falls as volume grows
items.explanation: Fixed cost is amortised across more units.

items.prompt: What is a 'diseconomy of scale'?
choices: Unit cost rising as volume grows
Unit cost falling as volume grows
items.explanation: The variable term grew faster than the fixed share shrank.

items.prompt: With $10,000 fixed and 1M orders, the fixed share per order is...
Which design choice tends to keep the variable term flat?
choices: Writing to the database on every request
Serving repeat reads from a cache
items.explanation: A cache avoids paying a growing database cost per request.

items.prompt: Service A paid a database write per request with no cache. Its curve...
items.explanation: Contention made each extra order costlier.

items.prompt: Which two things does the formula separate?
choices: Fixed cost and per-order variable cost
items.explanation: Those are the two terms in the model.

items.prompt: A service has $10,000 fixed and $0.02 variable per order. What is its cost per order at 5M orders?
items.reference:
The shape of cost per order
📐 cost per order = fixed / orders + variable per order
📉 constant variable: curve falls toward the variable term
📈 growing variable: curve can rise instead
Why: fixed cost is spread over more orders, but only a constant variable term lets that win.
items.learnMore:
Two terms, two stories

The fixed term always shrinks as volume grows. Whether the whole curve falls depends on whether the variable term stays flat.

Common mistake

Assuming growth alone makes unit cost fall.
items.reflection: Think of a bakery with one oven and a growing queue. When does adding customers make each loaf cheaper, and when does it make each loaf costlier?

items.prompt: A service's cost per order is rising while its fixed cost is constant. What must be true?
choices: The variable term outgrows the shrinking fixed share
Its fixed cost is secretly growing faster than volume
Its volume must in fact be falling during the period
Its formula stops applying once volume gets this high
items.explanation: The fixed share can only shrink; any rise has to come from the variable term.

items.prompt: In the model, what decides how many requests reach the database?
items.explanation: Only cache misses reach the database.

items.prompt: At 20M requests and an 80% hit ratio, how many are cache misses?
items.explanation: 20% of 20M is 4M.

items.prompt: With 14M reserved capacity and 20M requests, how many overflow?
items.explanation: 20M minus 14M is 6M.

items.prompt: Which cost is paid for every month regardless of traffic?
items.explanation: Reserved capacity is a flat monthly price.

items.prompt: Before the redesign, the monthly cost of this slice was about...
After the redesign, the monthly cost was about...
Database cost after the redesign (4M misses at $0.00026) is...
Which two levers did the redesign combine?
items.explanation: Cache cut misses; reservation cut overflow rates.

items.prompt: At 20M requests with a 50% hit ratio and the same prices, what is the database cost?
items.reference:
Two independent questions per request
🗄️ reached the database? decided by cache hit or miss
🖥️ which compute tier served it? decided by reserved capacity
💲 database cost = misses x $0.00026
💲 overflow cost = requests beyond reserved x $0.00034
Why: cache and reserved capacity are separate dimensions, so each is priced from its own count.
items.learnMore:
Price each dimension from its own count

Misses are counted from the hit ratio over all requests. Overflow is counted from requests beyond reserved capacity. They are never the same pool.

Common mistake

Using the overflow count to price database calls, or the miss count to price compute.
items.reflection: Think of a restaurant where one cost depends on whether the dish was pre-made and another on which cook made it. Why would mixing the two counts give a wrong bill?

items.prompt: With a 90% hit ratio at 20M requests, how does the database cost compare to the 80% case ($1,040)?
items.explanation: Misses halve from 4M to 2M, so cost halves.

items.prompt: Reserved capacity is billed...
choices: For every hour, used or not
items.explanation: That is why utilization matters.

items.prompt: On-demand capacity is billed...
choices: For every hour of the term
items.explanation: No commitment, pay per use.

items.prompt: Break-even utilization is calculated as...
choices: On-demand rate divided by reserved rate
Reserved rate divided by on-demand rate
items.explanation: Hours run x on-demand rate equals all hours x reserved rate.

items.prompt: With rates $0.05 reserved and $0.10 on-demand, break-even is...
An instance that runs above break-even is cheaper to...
items.explanation: Above break-even the flat rate beats pay per use.

items.prompt: An instance that runs well below break-even is cheaper...
items.explanation: Reserved would pay for mostly idle hours.

items.prompt: GreenCart's baseline tier runs about 90% of hours. Reserve or on-demand?
items.explanation: 90% is above the 60.4% break-even.

items.prompt: A sale-spike instance runs about 5% of a month. Reserve or on-demand?
items.explanation: 5% is far below break-even.

items.prompt: Reserved costs $0.06/hour and on-demand $0.10/hour. At what utilization are they equal?
items.explanation: 0.06 / 0.10 = 0.6; at 60% of hours both cost the same.
items.reference:
Reserved vs. on-demand, per instance
📦 reserved: $0.058 x 730 h = $42.34 every month
🖥️ on-demand at 90% use: $63.07
🖥️ on-demand at 5% use: $3.50
⚖️ break-even: 0.058 / 0.096 = 60.4% of hours
Why: reserved wins only when the instance runs more than the share of hours equal to the rate ratio.
items.learnMore:
Apply it per segment

The break-even is a property of one instance's utilization, not of the whole system. Apply it to the baseline tier and the spike tier separately.

Common mistake

Reading a big hourly discount as a reason to reserve everything.
items.reflection: Think of a gym membership versus paying per visit. How many visits a month would make the membership worthwhile, and how honestly do you forecast your visits?

items.prompt: Using $0.058 reserved and $0.096 on-demand over 730 hours, an instance runs 40% of the month. Which is cheaper?
choices: They are equal, at about $42 for each
items.explanation: On-demand: 0.096 x 730 x 0.4 = $28.03; reserved is a flat $42.34. 40% is below the 60.4% break-even.

The break-even is a property of one instance's utilization, not of the whole system. Apply it to the baseline tier and the spike tier separately.

Common mistake

Reading a big hourly discount as a reason to reserve everything.
items.reflection: Think of a gym membership versus paying per visit. How many visits a month would make the membership worthwhile, and how honestly do you forecast your visits?

items.prompt: A 40% hourly discount on reserved capacity is announced. Why is 'reserve everything' still wrong?
choices: The discount expires after the first month of use
It pays only on instances that run enough hours
Reserved instances run slower than the others do
Providers cap reservations at one instance each
items.explanation: The discount is multiplied by every hour, including idle ones.
items.reference:
Reserved vs. on-demand, per instance
📦 reserved: $0.058 x 730 h = $42.34 every month
🖥️ on-demand at 90% use: $63.07
🖥️ on-demand at 5% use: $3.50
⚖️ break-even: 0.058 / 0.096 = 60.4% of hours
Why: reserved wins only when the instance runs more than the share of hours equal to the rate ratio.

items.prompt: Right-sizing means...
choices: Always picking the smallest tier available to us
Paying for capacity that matches real load
items.explanation: Match capacity to observed need.

items.prompt: Which load should an instance be sized for?
items.explanation: The peak is where under-sizing hurts.

items.prompt: What is 'headroom'?
items.explanation: It absorbs the next spike.

items.prompt: Peak 22% of 8 vCPUs means about how many vCPUs are used?
Adding 20% headroom to 1.76 vCPUs gives about...
Is a 2-vCPU tier enough for a 2.11 vCPU requirement?
items.explanation: 2 is less than 2.11.

items.prompt: Which data do you need to right-size honestly?
items.explanation: Decisions need measurements.

items.prompt: Right-sizing mostly attacks which kind of waste?
choices: Idle capacity inside the fixed cost
items.explanation: You are paying for vCPUs nothing uses.

items.prompt: An instance with 4 vCPUs peaks at 30% CPU and the team wants 20% headroom. How many vCPUs are needed?
items.explanation: 0.30 x 4 = 1.2 used, times 1.2 = 1.44, so a 2-vCPU tier fits.
items.reference:
Size to peak plus headroom
📈 peak 22% of 8 vCPU = 1.76 vCPU used
🛟 plus 20% headroom = 2.11 vCPU needed
📏 2 vCPU is too small, 4 vCPU fits
💰 large $280.32 vs medium $140.16 per month
Why: size to the load you actually saw at peak with room to spare, because average sizing leaves no slack for the next spike.
items.learnMore:
Peak, not average

Average load hides the moments that matter. Size to peak plus headroom, then compare tiers on price.

Common mistake

Shrinking to the average and finding out at the next spike.
items.reflection: Think of a car you buy for the daily commute versus the yearly family trip. Which load do you size to, and what do you do about the rare peak?

It leaves no capacity for the next peak
